text: Education begins with stories, since children hear them before they train their bodies (Republic II, 377a–b). For that reason the founders must supervise the makers of stories, and Socrates gives two laws about what may be said of the gods. First, God is good and is cause only of good things; since evils far outnumber goods, some other cause must be found for them, because nothing good is harmful (379b–380c). This excludes Homer’s story of the two jars at Zeus’s threshold and every poet who makes a god responsible for the ruin of a household (379d–380a). Second, God neither changes nor deceives (380d–383c). Whatever is in the best condition is least changed by outside forces, and a perfect being would not willingly alter himself for the worse (381a–c). This excludes the old stories in which gods change their shape. The lie hated most by gods and human beings is not the spoken lie but the lie in the soul: being deceived about reality in the most important part of oneself (382a–b). A god has no such lie in himself and no motive to put one in another soul (382c–383a).
